txt: As she turns to face the sun reflected in the waves and the skyscrapers rising across the bay, you cannot help following her steady gaze.
Dark eyes survey the coast leading up to Martinaise. Dull grey metal rests in her scabbard -- a sword. The wind is too loud for her to hear...
Her eyes meet yours and suddenly she starts laughing. It's hoarse. As if she hasn't laughed in a while.
Say nothing? Well, now there's silence. She's looking at the sea. You hear yourself breathing.
She bursts out laughing. "Let's not get ahead of ourselves, now."
She bursts out laughing. "That's a good impression. You really crack me up, officer. Now how can I help you?"
She chuckles. "Drinking men aren't known for keeping their appointments."
She doesn't wait for an answer. You better get ready.
She just looks at you, her tea-length skirt flapping in the wind.
She looks around. "The kids sometimes go there too, I know they do -- on rafts. I tell them not to but they bring back old bullet casings and such."
She looks at the boat dripping with slush and nods, proudly.
She looks at you and shrugs. "This calls for a funeral if you ask me."
She nods to you, a playful glint in her eyes.
She nods. "I guess we wouldn't really *be* here if that thing wasn't on our team..."
She nods. "Please be conservative with the fuel, will you? I just filled her up, but it's a small tank."
She pulls out the papers. "Evrart and his plan for the village. I guess it does sound nice enough..."
She shakes her head, laughing. "You're just... what's the word -- *lamentable*, aren't you?"
She shrugs. "If you say so."
She thinks in silence, glances at the sea and finally speaks: "Aye, why not?"
She whistles quietly, picking at the fishnet at her feet. The wind ruffles her hair.
She's thinking, eyes mapping your rugged features. "Where would this... walk take us, officer?"
The crow's feet disappear from the corners of her eyes, as she smiles at you.
The wind ruffles her hair as she looks at the sunlit coast across the water.
The woman gazes steadily at the waves. A sudden gust picks up her dark hair and lets it fall again, tussled, wild. She brushes a few stray locks from her eyes, and only then spots you approaching.
There's a little pause. "So are you going to keep the name?"
There's a moment's silence. She looks at the rain streaming down the yellow belly of the boat.
There's a moment's silence. She looks at the slush-like rain-thing melt on the yellow belly of the boat.
There's a moment's silence. She looks at the slushy snow-melt on the yellow belly of the boat.
You both turn to consider the young woman. She's hunched over a net, methodically picking out ribbons of plastic...
"A *lot* of stuff," she concurs with a smile.
"A fishing village. On the seashore." She looks around. "This place doesn't really have a name. It's sometimes called... *Illisible*."
"A stroll on the beach sounds nice." She nods. "Alright, I guess I'll be seeing you at Land's End in the evening. When it gets dark, alright?"
"Absolutely." She nods. "Things like what for example?"
"Absurdly and pointedly phrased." She doesn't laugh. "You can be quite funny, officer. Anyway, what did you want?"
"Aha," she exclaims. "Like Snow Men!"
"Alcohol? Connect? I'm not sure I'm following you." There's confusion in her eyes.
"Alright, I will walk with you." She raises her finger. "But you need to understand that *nothing* is going to happen. We're just walking."
"Alright. I'll go put the kids to bed and we'll meet at Land's End in... fifteen minutes."
"Always seemed like there was something off about that islet to me..."
"And go where? The fish are plentiful here and we get enough orders to get by. It's not great, but it's something."
"And its people?" She bursts out laughing. "Glad to be of assistance then."
"And what about you? Keeping the name?"
"And why so? Our things are a part of our life-world. They're made with human sweat and they share human history. We should care about them as we care about humans, to some extent at least."
"Anyhow.... you also need Isobel's signature. If it's a bad idea, she won't sign. You'll find she's a tougher nut to crack than me."
"Anything I can help you with?"
"Anyway... you'll have to get Isobel to sign it too. I saw the signatories --  she won't if it's a bad idea. She's a much tougher nut to crack."
"Anyway..." She clears her throat. Twice. "I'd look near the fish market north of here, on the boardwalk. Drunks are *drawn* to markets, for some reason. Was there something else?"
"Are you now?" She smirks. "There are a lot of lawbringers around Martinaise, but not a lot of law."
"As for your 'paranatural abilities' -- I'd love to hear about them sometime, really, but can't we just enjoy the view for a moment?"
"Aye, I bet they are. The good ones at least."
"Aye, I guess you are." She nods. "I understand that's how it goes."
"Aye, I guess you do. What's on your mind, Officer Harry?"
"Aye, I guess you do. What's on your mind, officer?"
"Aye, always do... I like it. It's like being on another planet. A water planet. With water worries... and water joys."
"Aye, aye -- it's political." She stops you. "No need to step on a soapbox about it. What if we *disagree*?"
"Aye, but don't let it grow too much... this is not the place to settle down. Now, what's on your mind, Officer Harry?"
"Aye, but don't let it grow too much... this is not the place to settle down. Now, what's on your mind, officer?"
"Aye, by the looks of you, you do. Well, we're here now." She nods to you, a playful glint in her eyes.
"Aye, if you say so." She plucks on her net. "Probably better that way. I mean -- who likes construction noise?"
"Aye, ma'am... And it's a jetty, by the way."
"Aye, officer." A woman in a rain coat stands on the quay, considering an overturned boat. A sword in a scabbard hangs from her hip.
"Aye, so an officer should be. All that running around must need a lot of *structuring*..." She lets out a little laugh, as she turns to face the sun reflected in the waves.
"Aye, so here you are. Early in the morning and the sun is up." She breathes in the fresh air. "And not a drunk or teenager in sight. I'm surprised."
"Aye, so here you are. It's late and it's raining. The water is..." She puts her hands out and lets the rain fall on her palms. "Cold. Ice cold."
"Aye, so here you are. It's late and it's snowing. The snow is..." She extends her hand and catches a snowflake in her palm. "...Well, it's not really snow, it's slush."
"Aye, so here you are. It's late and the sun is going down. It'll be dark soon. If we stay here long enough we will be joined by a cortège of drunks and teenagers."
"Aye, so here you are. Mid-noon and the rain is..." She puts her hand in the rain, "...ice-cold as always. And it appears the drunks and teenagers haven't arrived yet."
"Aye, so here you are. Mid-noon and the snow is..." She catches a flake in her hand. "...well, it's not really snow, it's slush. At least the drunks and teenagers haven't joined us yet."
"Aye, so here you are. The sun is up and the rain is..." she puts her hand in the rain, "...cold. Ice cold. I don't mind. At least it keeps the drunks and teenagers at bay."
"Aye, so here you are. The sun is up and there's a ton of snow coming down." She catches a flake. "Well, it's not really snow, it's slush. At least it keeps the drunks and teenagers at bay."
"Aye, so here you are." She looks around. "I'm a bit surprised we're alone. It's mid-noon and the sun is out. I expected more drunks and teenagers. And drunk teenagers."
"Aye, the sea's gonna calm down soon. I can feel it. The wind is turning southeast." She nods. "What's on your mind, officer?"
"Aye, we all feel that way sometimes..." She turns her gaze towards the beach. "Sometimes I wonder if I'm the protagonist even in my own life story."
"Aye, you're the starriest of them all," she says with mock seriousness, then bursts out laughing as she turns to face the sun reflected in the waves.
"Aye," she nods. "And a benevolent one. When did you last have one of those on your side?"
"Aye," she nods.
"Aye. Brains, generally, aren't very good, are they? I prefer backs, arms, shoulders -- lungs, too." She smiles. "You know..."
"Aye. Feels deserved, don't you think? Falling in the line of duty like that and all."
"Aye. No one wants to talk about how frightened they are. But only frightened people are *really* dangerous -- and *plenty* of them are dangerous."
"Aye." She looks at the rain circles on the water. "*Sunny* days. You got a problem with that?"
"Aye." She looks at the snow melt in the water. "*Sunny* days. You got a problem with that?"
"Aye." She nods solemnly. "I've always taken you for one, that's for sure. Not a lot of RCM men who aren't killers."
"Aye." She nods solemnly. "Not a lot of RCM men who aren't killers."
"Aye." She nods. "I better head home to the kids."
"Be careful out there. Sea's calm as death, but still... there are ruins underwater. You can scrape the paint... or worse."
"Be my guest." She looks at the boys. "They've a strange way of talking. See if you can get anything *useful* out of them. I seldom do..."
"Besides, you also need Isobel's signature," she says with a smile. "If it's a bad idea, she won't sign."
"Bottles. Drugs, also. Lost cargo in general." She looks at the beach. "But most of the time, it's just wood and glass."
"But daydreaming is a rich man's game. At sea you can't afford to be careless and dream. Anyway..." She shakes her head. "What are we talking about here again?"
"But until that happens I can try to assist you the best I can," she adds with a smile. "So, what will it be, officer?"
"Can't wait to hear it." She smirks and turns toward the sunlit sea.

"Charming. My man was like that too. Had to knock two of his teeth out to establish a good relationship dynamic." She chuckles. "I'll see you at Land's End in the evening. Be there after dark, alright?"
"Charming. My man was like that too. Had to knock two of his teeth out to establish a good relationship dynamic." She chuckles. "I'll see you at Land's End in... let's say fifteen minutes."
"Do they? Some of them do but..." She shrugs. "Sounds to me like you should choose your allies better, that's all."
"Doesn't look like nothing. Looks like you got banged up real good."

"Don't have any," she replies with a shrug. "Those get cleaned out so fast even the local bums can only stand by and watch with watery mouths. Always by strangers too. Union folk don't stand this kind of stuff around here."
"Doubt it." She smiles sadly. "But thank you for the company."
"Drying out? Becoming religious?" Her face is serious for a moment, but then she smiles warmly. "To hell with it. I'm not going to lecture you about your drinking, not here."
"Eh..." she looks confused. "What?"
"Everyone does that, in a way. You don't have to get shot for that." She waves her hand dismissively.
"Exactly." She tries to smile and reaches in her net. "I don't mean to complain about my sad pauper life. We do manage alright. We're tough people here."
"Farewell." She nods to you and turns to go.
"Fine by me." She brushes her hair aside, waiting for you to speak.
"Fine," she replies with a shrug. "The date is dropped. Now what else can we discuss?"
"Fine." The pen clicks. "Here you go."

"From time to time people need a lesson in respect. That's just the way it is. Back in the day I caught the eyes of many men and believe me," she adds, tittering, "men need a lesson in manners from time to time."
"Funny. Funny sailor jokes." She nods, without smiling. "Sorry if I'm not laughing out loud, but the comedy has worn thin over the years."
"Go right ahead." She looks at you, head slightly tilted.
"Goddamnit... I *just* bought that net..."
"Gone."
"Good one. I'm gonna go with *the rope*."
"Good. 'Twould have been bad news had it turned out it wasn't a sunny day. Bad news for the skiff. Bad news for the nets. Bad news for the kids."
"Guess I enjoyed the way he bled." Her expression doesn't change. It's hard to say if it's a joke.
"Guns are expensive... and fragile. I think." She shrugs. "Besides, I got kids. Can't have guns around them and sometimes a sharp blade is enough to keep folks at bay."
"Ha! It's enough that my fish goes there. Fifty reál a piece they ask for spring cod..."
"Have this. The sun's good but it doesn't *stick* things -- I've no use for it anymore."
"He didn't respect the sea. Went out there drunk like a skunk and sure enough one day the boat was found floating empty. The bloated corpse turned up two weeks later."
"He has a pen and everything..." She takes it from you, a doubtful look in her eyes, clicks it and places the tip on the paper.
"Here it comes," she says. As she turns back to the sea, the weather begins to clear under her steady gaze.
"Here you go."
"Hey, kids! Oh... never mind."
"Hm, an installation?" She raises her eyebrows. "Us poor people are stupid and don't get 'installations'. All I see is a heap of trash. This actually calls for a funeral, I think."
"Holding a funeral doesn't mean you love death. Don't be childish. You're a police officer..."
"Huh... haven't seen the RCM around for ages."
"Hundreds. Maybe thousands even..." She looks around. "The kids sometimes go there too, I know they do. On barges. I tell them not to but they bring back old bullet casings and such."
"I apologize," she replies with a nod. "It looked like you could face-down any horror in the world with that unchanging grin. Looked like a shield."
"I buried my man, mourned for a month and that was it. Life didn't really change that much for me and the kids. Not for the worse at least."
"I do, yes. A stroll on the beach sounds nice, doesn't it?" She nods. "Alright. I'll see the kids haven't killed each other and we'll meet at Land's End in... fifteen minutes?"

"I don't mean to complain about my pauper life. We are warm and fed here and..." She smiles faintly and plucks some seaweed out of the net. "I don't know, there's just something about this shit hole."
"I don't really know. Further down the peninsula I guess. I mean that's where they were heading." She points north. "Who else are you looking for, beside Snow Men?"
"I don't. But us working folk don't have the luxury to be bed-sick with melancholy." She crosses her arms. "I buried him, mourned for an appropriate amount of time and went on."
"I guess men with authority have their quirks." She waves you off. "What brings you here, Lawbringer?"
"I guess that makes you into some sort of a terrier." She picks on her net. "Either way, I can't help you out."
"I have and I don't really..." She hesitates.
"I really need to get out there, catch something."
"I see you haven't left our little Martinaise yet. Still running around," she observes. "Like some kind of cross-country law official."
"I sell the fish to people in the Delta to serve at their fancy restaurants. Authentic Insulindian cuisine."
"I shouldn't have?"
"I understand, believe me, I really do." She brushes back her hair. "I think about all the frivolous side-activities I *could* be doing every time I go out there with my nets."
"I'm sad to hear that. Take care of that with ether, will you? Don't get too many RCM men around here. Be sad to lose the first one."

"I'm sure you have," she replies with a peculiar look. "I don't have to hear about it, but I do wish you luck finding the thing. Look near the fish market north of here, on the boardwalk. Drunks are *drawn* to markets."
"I've seen quite few of those first days, aye. Still, good for you..." She nods to you, a playful glint in her eyes.
"If one of 'em lost something, that's as good a place to start looking as any."
"If you promise to bring it back. And no scraping the hull -- I just got it nice and yellow. And *no* drinking on the boat." Her eyes narrow. "And no joyriding, either."
"In time," she replies with a nod and adds: "When the sea turns and the winds settle she will be ready."
"Intense." She pulls her fingers through her hair. "You're like some kind of dark terrier with your endless searches. Maybe there's something else I can help you with then?"
"Is this from the shooting in town?" She's not letting it go that easy. "We heard gunshots. Not that we don't hear gunshots all the time, but they were closer than usual."

"Isn't it strange," she breaks the silence abruptly, "For this all-powerful thing, the sun... to be so generous towards us? You know, the best time to go out fishing is usually toward sunset, when the water is warmer..."
"It didn't suck," she smiles. "I'll let you get back to your business now. The twins probably found a land mine by now..."
"It's a common Revacholian expression." She narrows her eyes. "Means drinking yourself to death."
"It's a good thing too that he has an actual police officer looking for it." A smile lights up her face. "Good old Doom Spiral, upper-management to the core."
"It's a regular mass-produced sword, like a shovel or an axe. Nothing fancy, just for intimidation."

"It's bringing us spring, summer... It's entirely on our side, no matter what we do or who we are. For absolutely *no* reason. It's unlike no other powerful being -- certainly no powerful organisation, or government? How can that be?"
"It's kinda nice seeing cops around..."
"It's no bother. Don't get many excuses to spend time alone, what with my trio of monsters..."
"It's yellowfin season soon."
"Johnny what now?" She's trying to resist a smile. "That's not proper cop behaviour, is it?"
"Just a walk?!" She feigns extreme surprise. "I don't know, officer -- I would not have taken you for an innocent perambulator."
"Knew the weather'd clear up once we got here -- otherwise it would've been a less pleasant stroll, nay?"

"Know that you're not the first guy to bring a girl to Land's End. This is what locals call a *make-out spot*. That is not going to happen here today -- I just want to make that clear, dimples." She turns to face the sea once more.
"Let's just admire this piece of the world we happen to have in front of us, a?" She nods to you, a playful glint in her eyes.
"Let's see," she tilts her head ever so slightly. "Who are you looking for?"
"Life didn't really change that much for me and the kids..." She glances at the village where two little kids are playing with what look like rocks.
"Like I said, fish, mostly. Sail the waves, take care of the kids. Pick nets... right now I'm tarring a little skiff."
"Look at you, you can barely walk!"
"Me too," she replies with sudden sincerity. "It's been ages since I just had normal conversation with one of you guys."
"Me? No, no, no." She laughs. "Just grew up on the sea. Know which way the wind's blowing and all."
"Men with authority have their quirks. Comes with never being second-guessed about anything..." She waves you off.

"Mhm, used to be some kind of fortification there before the war -- for the communards. An anti-aircraft gun, I think. Bombed to bits in the landing... I haven't been there myself -- always steered clear of it."
"My husband used to drink there. Him and his drinking buddies. Always seemed like a bad place to drink to me. People died there during the landing, you know -- my mother told me..."
"My husband used to drink there. Him and his drinking buddies. Always seemed like a bad place to drink to me. People died there during the landing, you know, my mother told me..."
"No, I'm afraid not." Her eyes are smiling as her hand moves to the hilt. "Attempting to confiscate the blade I use to keep these animals in check? You would put me in an early grave."
"No, no. There's nothing to find. He's dead. Lost to the waves."
"No. Men around here are too drunk to pose a threat to me."
"No." She smirks. "And it will outlive them all."
"Not really." She glances at the blade. "I know some basic moves and I know it sure as hell beats a knife, when you're in a tough spot."
"Not the best use of your time, is it, Mr. Lawman? Harassin' homeless people on the beach and the like..."

"Nothing, just ruins. Used to be some kind of fortification there before the war, for the communards. An anti-aircraft gun, I think. Bombed to bits in the landing... I haven't been there myself -- always steered clear of it."
"Now there's a whole shipment of big words." She looks at you from head to toe. "May mankind be plentiful, I guess? Can I get back to my nets now?"
"Now you're just being another kind of fool." She laughs, a playful glint in her eyes. "You should know -- I don't spend time with people out of any sense of obligation."
"Now you're just nitpicking." She smiles. "But aye, I concede -- maybe *desert people* sometimes disagree."
"Now, before you tell me how sorry you are for my loss, know that it was four years ago and I've moved on. There's only so much mourning you can do for a drunk with sinewy muscles."
"Of course. Can I help you with something?"
"Officer Harry, what happened? You're limping. Why are you limping? You look terrible."
"Officer Harry... you're wounded. Why are you wounded? You look terrible."
"Officer, what happened? You're limping. Why are you limping? You look terrible."
"Officer, what happened? You're wounded. Why are you wounded? You look terrible."
"Oh indeed."
"Oh no, *you* come with us. Seriously, I insist." She smiles at the lieutenant and turns back to you...
"Oh yeah," she says with a chuckle. "You won't even be able to get it out of the water before early June and where are you gonna bury it? Who to invite? What music to play at the wake?"
"Oh, but of course -- why didn't I think of that?" She rolls her eyes. "Look, I have mouths to feed and as much as I'd like a change, I... they need stability first."
"Oh, that was a bit of pride, and a bit of superstition..."
"Oh, very." She laughs. "Finding pieces of glass, bits of wood. Every once in a while we get dead bodies -- human, animal, fish, other sea creatures. A mine washed ashore, once..."

"Oh," she chuckles. "There's plenty missing, but that's too much for even an eager terrier like you to handle. Although you seem very thorough. Tell me instead, is there something else I can help you with?"
"Oh..." She looks slightly disappointed. "I've been out on the sea for most of the past week. The weather's been good for fishing, so I usually start at four in the morning."
"Oh..." She shakes her head, smiling faintly. "Believe *me*, everyone here is a 'proper' man. Must be something about poverty that makes all the men *real*."
"Oh..." she looks at the pointed direction. "That's good to know, I guess. Why is it in the sea?"
"Oh? The kids too, right?" She doesn't wait for your reply. "Working class people don't have that luxury. That's for rich folks. We just go on."
"Oh? Who?"
"Okay, when did this person stay here?"
"Okay." She blinks. "Where is this going?"
"Our things are a part of our life-world. They're made with human sweat and they share human history. We should care about them as we care about humans. To some extent at least," she adds.

"People imagine picking up and finding *something better* is an easy solution. But how is that supposed to work, when all your time and energy goes to staying alive? You have almost nothing to set aside to actually fight your way out."
"Police business. I understand." She nods. "Anything I can help you with?"

"Probably." She smiles. "But it is a youth centre and I have children. Got to give them *something* else to do. They're cute and small now, but they're growing up fast. I had my first drink when I was eleven, because I was so bored..."
"Quite the sign. An eye-sore too." She frowns. "The situation calls for a funeral if you ask me."
"Really? Are you sure you're not also looking for Nadia Harnankur? Or Ignus Nilsen? Or the great lost city of Eis under the waves?"
"Remarkable..." She shakes her head. "That one already lost everything else and now his jacket too?"
"Right," she nods. "Not only Snow Men -- also Green Men, Monkey Men, burning rhinos. You get the picture."
"See, that makes me not want to lend you my skiff. On a boat, *rocking* leads to capsizing. That there is an absolutely one-hundred percent *rock-free* skiff, you got that?"
"So now that you know -- you keeping the name?"
"So this is what this is -- responsible?" She shrugs. "Well... maybe it is. Maybe you'll have a *revelation* and crack whatever you're on."
"So what brings you here, Lawbringer?"
"So you're a killer." She nods solemnly. "That's good, I guess. I guess... Better than being dead."
"Some went to patch their wounds, their lesson learned, others were more thick-headed..." She looks down. "And one of them I ended up marrying."
"Sometimes I also walk the beach to see what the sea has given up. The sea is full of surprises."
"Sorry I couldn't help you out." A faint smile runs across her face. "Maybe I can help you find someone else?"
"Sure is. *The Sun* I call her. Coated with a fresh layer of tar just yesterday. It'll take some time for it to dry, assuming the sunny days continue."
"Sure it is. 'Twould be bad news for the skiff if it weren't. Bad news for the nets. Bad news for the kids."
"Sure, but it's temporary and for a good cause and I need to give the children *something* else to do..."

"Sure, sure... that makes it alright." She rolls her eyes, but then suddenly a smile appears. "Still, I do hope you find it. Look near the fish market north of here, on the boardwalk. Drunks are *drawn* to markets."
"Sure." Her face straightens. "It looks as if you could face-down any horror in the world with that same unchanging grin. It's like a shield."
"Take it from someone who's been through a few funerals: It's easiest to just leave them there and let nature take care of it."
"Thank you. I'm half Ubi. My mother was from Ubi Sunt?. Not a lot of sun there, I hear, though I've never been..."
"Thank you. Out there on the other planet -- the sea -- you start seeing things in a strange light. I'm glad I got to share it." She smiles. "You know..."
"That Evrart and the Union have nice plans for anything. I thought they only cared about themselves." She shakes her head. "Well, I guess Union members have children too."
"That goes for men too, but they put on an act for us. Pretend like everything's good and living in shit doesn't bother them. Like anyone falls for that."
"That it does. But then... we are also enemies to our enemies, eh? And so she shines on us. The cops and the commies, the killers and the saints. You know..."
"That won't be a problem. It's windstill -- and the tar just dried." She points to her skiff next to the jetty. "We've got two days of *relative* sunshine ahead."
"That's great." The woman glances towards the wreckage again. "Until then you should maybe start thinking about the funeral?"
"That's nothing to brag about, officer."

"That's sweet of you. It really is. I'd check around the abandoned fish market on the boardwalk. Drunks are inexplicably drawn to markets... might be why they have such trouble staying in business..."

"That's what I asked *you*." She tilts her head. "It's a youth centre and I have children. Got to give them *something* else to do. They're cute and small now, but they're growing up fast. I had my first drink when I was eleven, because I was so bored..."
"The name is Lilienne. People call me Net Picker." She gestures toward the fishnets. "I think I have time for questions. And that was actually the second one."
"The name is Lilienne. People call me Net Picker." She gestures toward the fishnets. "I think I have time for questions. What are the other ones?"
"The sign on the street leading here is *illegible*. Has been since they built this place." The wind rattles her earrings.
"The throw-nets just aren't paying off this time of the year..."
"The twins." She points to the two kids playing on the concrete yard. "God forbid they bring the girl along on a rickety barge."
"The twins." She points to the two kids playing on the concrete yard. "God forbid they bring the girl along on some rickety barge."
"The waves are beginning to die down... look at those little bastards. Simmer down. Simmer down, bastards."
"The wind's gonna pick up soon and I have to go, but..." She takes her sword out of the scabbard. The blade reflects the sunlight, a dark orange.
"The world?" She laughs. "Those big words men like to throw around as though they had weight."
"These?" she turns her head and they dangle. "These aren't real fish-hooks, silly. They're earrings shaped to look like fish-hooks. A drunk called Rosemary brought them to me. I kept them."
"They're cute and small now, but they're growing up fast. Too fast, I had my first drink when I was eleven, because I was so bored..."
"Thought you guys forgot this place even exists."
"To the waves." Her eyes stop in yours. "The sea took him. It was a long time ago."
"Two odd guys have been wandering around here, nose in sand, talking nonsense about Snow Men and the like."
"Ugh... sure. Venomosity." She nods. "But boys will be boys and god knows we don't have many around. So far the sword has been enough to keep them in line."
"Ugh..." She frowns, thinking. "I don't think I know what these are. Care to elaborate?"
"Uh..." She raises an eyebrow. "Good for you. He, however, was lost to the waves. It's been quite a while now."
"Unbelievable, you *are* looking for more lost things." She smiles. "Doom Spiral losing his jacket on the other hand is *very* believable. I mean he has lost everything else already."
"Unfortunately, the factory sold this one with a three-year warranty instead of a story." She smiles at her own joke. "It's to intimidate folks, mostly."
"Us working folk don't have the luxury to be bed-sick with melancholy." She crosses her arms. "I buried him, mourned for an appropriate amount of time, and went on."
"Wait, do you think *I* did that? Nay, I just grew up on the sea, that's all. Know which way the wind is blowing."
"Wasn't feeling it," she repeats thoughtfully. "That calls for a funeral if you ask me."
